scenes.narration: [HL 1] The for line has three parts. A loop name, i. The word in. And range of five. Python ties i to zero and runs the block. Then it ties i to one, then two, up to the last number. [HL 2] The block prints the step number. Notice we never wrote i equals i plus one. The for loop does that for us. [HL 3] This line is at the left edge, so it runs once, after the loop ends.

scenes.narration: Here is a small surprise. After the loop ends, the name i is still there. It stays tied to the last value it received, four. The for loop made the name, and tied it to each value in turn. It does not tidy the name away when the loop finishes. That is normal Python, and it is useful to know.

scenes.narration: [HL 1] [TRACK n=1] Range with two numbers gives a start and a stop. Start at one, stop before six. So n takes the values one to five. [HL 2] Each round prints a line of the five times table. The sum inside print is worked out each time. [TRACK n=5] The last line is, five times five equals twenty five. A start and a stop is how you ask for exactly the numbers you want.

code.source:
for n in range(1, 6):
    print("5 x", n, "=", 5 * n)

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: an off-by-one range
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We want the numbers one to five. We wrote range of one, five. The output stops at four. Python does not include the stop value. Five is the stop, so it is left out. To include five, the stop must be six. This is called an off by one bug, and every programmer meets it.

props.why: range stops before its stop value, so to include 5 the stop must be 6.

shorts.title: What is range?
shorts.hook: "The range function makes a series of numbers."
shorts.script: The range function makes a series of numbers. Range of five gives zero, one, two, three, four. Five numbers, but it starts at zero. The stop value is never included. Think of stepping stones across a stream. Range lays out the stones, and a for loop steps on each one in turn. Whenever you know how many times to repeat, for and range are your friends. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Numbers to loop over.

shorts.title: Start and stop
shorts.hook: "Range can take a start and a stop."
shorts.script: Range can take a start and a stop. Range of one, six gives one, two, three, four, five. It starts at one, and stops before six. So the last number is always one less than the stop. If you want one to ten, write range of one, eleven. Read it as, from one, up to but not including eleven. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Stop is not included.

shorts.title: The loop name
shorts.hook: "In a for loop, Python makes the loop name for you."
shorts.script: In a for loop, Python makes the loop name for you. For i in range of five. I is tied to zero, then one, then two, up to the last number. You never write i equals i plus one. The loop does it. After the loop ends, i is still there, tied to the last value, which is four. Handy to know when you debug. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Python moves i for you.

shorts.title: Off by one
shorts.hook: "Here is the most famous bug in loops."
shorts.script: Here is the most famous bug in loops. You want the numbers one to five, so you write range of one, five. The output stops at four. Range does not include the stop value. To get five, the stop must be six. Programmers call this an off by one bug. Whenever a loop runs one time too few, check the stop value first. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Check the stop value.
